claims.text: Thermal energy induces local elemental segregation during premelting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Local elemental segregation creates heterogeneous configurational-energy landscapes within these nanoparticles.
The heterogeneous energy landscape delays the melting behavior relative to chemically uniform, simpler nanoparticles.
The heterogeneous energy landscape alters the melting behavior relative to chemically uniform, simpler nanoparticles.
The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
Controlled in situ heating and cooling combined with time-resolved TEM or synchrotron X-ray diffraction can monitor phase and elemental evolution.
Local elemental segregation produces spatial variation in interatomic bond energies among nanoparticle subdomains.
Heating causes subtle elemental redistribution within the chemically complex alloy.
Elemental redistribution creates localized regions having different melting points.
Regions with different local melting points postpone or otherwise alter the overall melting transition.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit a delayed onset of complete melting relative to the baseline nanoparticles.
The high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit transient elemental-segregation patterns or intermediate phase boundaries during heating.
The simpler baseline nanoparticles will undergo a comparatively uniform melting transition.
The proposed mechanism is limited to temperatures near and above the solidus where atomic reconfiguration can occur without rapid destruction of the solid solution.
The extent of segregation and its effect on melting dynamics may depend on nanoparticle size.
The extent of segregation and its effect on melting dynamics may depend on heating rate and atomic-diffusion kinetics.
